conflict_topics: smell affecting laundry in service yard
living-room exposure/ability to work from home
dialogue_quality_notes: Speakers provide concrete reasons: A cites work and video calls (Turn 5); C cites laundry absorption (Turn 3); D cites cultural/food identity (Turn 4).
Repeated, focused requests: Agent B repeatedly asks for advance warning (Turns 6, 8, 9, 18).
Partial concession introduced by D: "what if I only cook it once a week?" (Turn 21) shifts the conversation toward negotiation.
No resolution and some role diffusion: negotiation appropriately involves all parties but Agent C's preferred solution is not elaborated after raising the laundry issue.
evaluation.final_reason: No mutually accepted, concrete agreement was reached. D offered a concession: "what if I only cook it once a week?" and A proposed Saturday: "What about on Saturday? I'm usually out then." B consistently said a warning is sufficient: "If I get a warning, I can close my door." These proposals were not harmonized into a single, mutually accepted rule and Agent C's laundry concern remains unaddressed.
position_change_notes: Agent D softened from defending cultural cooking (Turn 4) to offering a frequency concession: "what if I only cook it once a week?" (Turn 21).
Agent A moved from a blanket request (no strong-smelling food) to a conditional acceptance of once-a-week on a specific day: "What about on Saturday?" (Turn 22).
Agent B remained consistent: primary need is an advance warning so they can close their door: "If I get a warning, I can close my door." (Turn 25).
Agent C consistently raised the laundry impact early (Turn 3) but did not state a preferred solution later in the transcript.

round_scores.evidence: Agent B: "My room is next to the kitchen. The smell really gets into everything." Agent C: "My laundry is drying just outside. It picks up the smell too." — grievances about cooking smell create an active, shared incompatibility.

Agent D: "This is the food I eat. The food I grew up with." vs Agent A: "...the smell is very strong... I work here. I have video calls with clients." — competing claims (personal/cultural food practice vs. work/quiet living-room requirement) increase the substantive conflict.

Agent B: "What if you open the kitchen window and use the hood? And if you tell us before you cook, we can close our doors." Agent D: "I do use the hood and open the window. The hood isn't very strong." — proposed mitigations meet a structural limitation; disagreement persists.

Agent B: "...let us know before you start? Then I can close my door." Agent C: "That doesn't help the laundry." — introduces multiple incompatible needs (door-closers vs. laundry exposure), broadening the dispute.

Agent D: "So no one else cooks anything with a strong smell?" Agent A: "It's the sambal, Agent D. That smell is very strong, and it stays in the air for hours." — defensive pushback and restatement of the core problem; no settlement.

Agent D: "So if someone boils herbs or stock for hours, that smell is okay?" Agent A: "That's not the same. Those smells don't stick to the furniture for hours." — continued factual/normative disagreement about the nature and impact of smells.

Agent B repeats: "Agent D, can you just let us know before you start?" Agent D: "And what about Agent C's laundry?" — the simple request meets an unresolved cross-interest (laundry), so conflict remains.
Agent B: "That's a different problem. I'm asking if you can let me know..." Agent C: "It's the same smell, Agent B." — parties articulate incompatible problem framings; no agreement reached.

Agent B: "...can you just give a warning? That's all I'm asking." Agent D: "So if I agree, is this a new house rule for everyone? We all warn each other before we cook anything with a strong smell?" — the issue broadens to household rules and fairness, increasing the stakes and opposing positions.

Agent A: "A warning doesn't help the living room. There's no door to close." Agent D: "Okay, what if I only cook it once a week?" — D offers a concrete concession (frequency limit), which reduces but does not resolve incompatible preferences about timing and affected spaces.

Agent A: "Once a week is better, but it's still a problem if it's on a weekday. What about on Saturday? I'm usually out then." Agent D: "And what works for Agent B and Agent C?" — negotiation continues; some softening but unresolved because others' preferences not yet integrated.

Agent A: "So, does Saturday work?" Agent B: "The day of the week doesn't matter to me. If I get a warning, I can close my door. That's all I need." — incompatible preferred solutions remain (A wants Saturday; B wants warning; C's laundry concern not settled).

substantive_insights: Mitigations address different subsets of harms: an advance warning helps those who can close doors (B) but does not address communal spaces or laundry (A and C).
Structural constraints (weak hood, landlord forbids changes, shared laundry area) limit effective technical fixes.

Positions are grounded in differing interests: cultural practice and dietary needs (D) vs. work requirements (A) and property cleanliness (C), so simple one-size rules are unlikely to satisfy everyone.
D's proposal to cook only once a week is a credible concession but requires coordination (day/time) that has not been agreed.
